newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hughes' Armstrong says not in talks on AT&T post.
newsitem.headline: Hughes' Armstrong says not in talks on AT&T post.

text.p: The executive tipped in U.S. media reports to take over as president of AT&T Corp said on Wednesday he intends to stay in his present job.
Michael Armstrong, head of U.S. firm Hughes Electronics Corp, flatly denied speculation that he would be picked as president of the U.S. long-distance carrier this week.

"It is just not true that I am in discussions with AT & T. I haven't been contacted by the company and I haven't been offered the job," Armstrong, in Tokyo on Hughes business, told Reuters in an interview.
"I am very happy and intend to stay with Hughes...because it's a fantastic company," he said.
Asked if he would take the job if it was offered, he said: "I haven't the faintest idea."
Alex Mandl abruptly resigned as AT & T president in August to take up a post in a small telephone company.
Armstrong, who has successfully restructured Hughes into a consumer company from a defence contractor, emerged in U.S. media this week as the leading candidate for the job.
He also denied market talk that Hughes hoped to become independent of its biggest shareholder, General Motors Corp.
"It used to be true. Because we needed to have a greater liquidity or stock, we were hopeful to get a more knowledgeable governance of our company," he said.

But from Hughes' perspective "the problem was solved", he said. Over the past four years, Hughes had increased its liquidity and now had its own board of directors who had been given a delegated authority, he said.
"The GM board has been very supportive of all of our investments as we diversified the company and have gone much more heavily in telecommunications," Armstrong said.

For months Wall Street has speculated that GM may want to spin off Hughes, which the carmaker acquired in 1985 for more than $5 billion. Analysts have said that the rapidly changing Hughes no longer fits in GM's mix of business.

Armstrong, who left for the United States later on Wednesday, was in Tokyo to announce that DirecTV Japan Inc, a group company of Hughes Electronics, would start a digital satellite broadcasting service in Japan in autumn 1997.
He did not rule out the possibility that DirecTV might link up with Japanese broadcasters, saying "all options are available to us". AT&T owns 2.5 percent of DirecTV.
